z-m-35-01.title: A solution saying that the number of students who applied for neither is 20
z-m-35-01.topic: The complement of a union and an intersection, and the number of elements
z-m-35-01.goal: Find in one line of a solution the error that arises when translating 'neither ... nor ...' into set notation and fix it, and say who the same calculation actually counts.
z-m-35-01.material: Let the 24 students of a class be the universal set U. In the after-school sign-up, let A be the set of students who signed up for soccer (13 students) and B the set of students who signed up for basketball (10 students), and 4 students signed up for both. A student may sign up for both, or for neither. Jisu tried to find 'the number of students who signed up for neither soccer nor basketball' and solved it as follows. (How to read the symbols: Aᶜ is 'the complement of A', ∪ is 'union', ∩ is 'intersection', n(A) is 'the number of elements of A'.)
z-m-35-01.thinking.0: Finding the first line of the solution that goes wrong
z-m-35-01.thinking.1: Interpreting whom the calculated value is counting
z-m-35-01.thinking.2: Checking the result by another method
z-m-35-01.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty label for the production batch, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes the learner has already studied the 'sets and propositions' unit of high school Common Mathematics once (operations on sets, the proposition 'if p then q', and counterexamples).
z-m-35-01.prereq.1: Can use the relationship between the numbers of elements of two sets (inclusion and exclusion).
z-m-35-01.prereq.2: Knows that 'and' and 'or' correspond to the intersection and union of sets.
z-m-35-01.s.s1.prompt: Where is the first line in Jisu's solution at which the thinking goes wrong? Line numbers are counted from 1.
z-m-35-01.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one student. For example, check whether 'a student who signed up only for basketball' is in the set in line 1.
z-m-35-01.s.s1.hint.1: Separately decide whether that student is also one of 'the students who signed up for neither soccer nor basketball', which the problem asks for, and compare the two decisions.
z-m-35-01.s.s1.line.0: 'Students who signed up for neither soccer nor basketball' are 'students who did not sign up for soccer' or 'students who did not sign up for basketball', so the set we want is Aᶜ∪Bᶜ.
z-m-35-01.s.s1.line.1: But Aᶜ∪Bᶜ is the same as (A∩B)ᶜ.
z-m-35-01.s.s1.line.3: So the number of students who signed up for neither soccer nor basketball is 20.
z-m-35-01.s.s1.explain: Joining 'did not sign up for soccer nor basketball' with 'or' in line 1 is where it first goes wrong. To sign up for neither, it must be 'did not sign up for soccer and also did not sign up for basketball', so it is Aᶜ∩Bᶜ, that is, (A∪B)ᶜ. Aᶜ∪Bᶜ=(A∩B)ᶜ in line 2 holds by itself and the calculation in line 3 (24−4=20) is also correct, but the set chosen in line 1 is different, so the conclusion in line 4 is wrong.
z-m-35-01.s.s2.prompt: The 20 Jisu found is the number of which students? Choose the best explanation of the students that the calculation 24 − 4 is actually counting.
z-m-35-01.s.s2.hint.0: Make a table of how many students signed up only for soccer, only for basketball, and for both.
z-m-35-01.s.s2.hint.1: Out of all 24, write down by group which kinds of students are in the 20 left after subtracting 4.
z-m-35-01.s.s2.o.a: All the students who signed up for neither soccer nor basketball
z-m-35-01.s.s2.r.a: You read the target Jisu first meant to find as it is. Check whether students who signed up only for basketball are in the 20.
z-m-35-01.s.s2.o.b: Students who did not sign up for both
z-m-35-01.s.s2.r.b: You read exactly, as a set, who is left when only the 4 students who signed up for both are subtracted from everyone.
z-m-35-01.s.s2.o.c: Students who signed up for exactly one
z-m-35-01.s.s2.r.c: 'Exactly one' must exclude both the students who signed up for both and the students who signed up for neither. Check whether it is the same as the calculation that subtracts only 4 from 24.
z-m-35-01.s.s2.o.d: Students who signed up for soccer and did not sign up for basketball
z-m-35-01.s.s2.r.d: Those students are the part of A with A∩B removed. Check whether that fits with the calculation using 24 starting from everyone.
z-m-35-01.s.s2.explain: 24−4 subtracts only the 4 students who signed up for both from everyone, so it is the sum of soccer only (13−4=9 students) + basketball only (10−4=6 students) + students who signed up for neither. 9+6+(5 students who signed up for neither)=20, which equals the number of elements of (A∩B)ᶜ.
z-m-35-01.s.s3.prompt: Tell Jisu. In one or two sentences, write which line of the solution should be fixed and how, how many students signed up for neither soccer nor basketball after fixing it, and how you checked that this number is right.
z-m-35-01.s.s3.hint.0: First, apply the 'or' in line 1 as a sentence to one student, and decide what it should be changed to.
z-m-35-01.s.s3.hint.1: After finding the number of elements of the fixed set, add the numbers of students who signed up only for soccer, only for basketball, and for both, and check that it matches 24.
z-m-35-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: In line 1, ..., so it is ... students. Checking, ...
z-m-35-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I explain in my own words why 'neither ... nor ...' is joined with 'and'?
z-m-35-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I check the value 5 once more with another calculation (for example 24−19, or adding by group)?
z-m-35-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I also point out whom the 20 counts?
z-m-35-01.s.s3.model.0: Line 1 has to be fixed. To sign up for neither, it is 'not soccer and not basketball', so it is Aᶜ∩Bᶜ, that is, (A∪B)ᶜ. n(A∪B)=13+10−4=19, so 24−19=5 students. Adding soccer only 9, basketball only 6, and both 4 also gives 19, so it fits.
z-m-35-01.s.s3.model.1: 'Neither ... nor ...' should be joined with 'and' and not 'or', so line 1 becomes Aᶜ∩Bᶜ. The answer is 5 students. Check: soccer only 9 + basketball only 6 + both 4 + neither 5 = 24, which matches the total.
z-m-35-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer checked by adding by group instead of using the union formula.

z-m-35-02.title: If not a single student goes against it, is the notice true?
z-m-35-02.topic: Truth and falsity of a proposition, and the case where no element satisfies the condition
z-m-35-02.goal: Use the fact that the truth of 'if p then q' is decided by whether there is a counterexample to adjust your judgment and confidence when no element satisfies p and when a new element arrives, and say why.
z-m-35-02.material: A school library has the notice 'Every student who is 190 cm or taller uses reading room B'. Let p be 'is 190 cm or taller' and q be 'uses reading room B', and examine the proposition 'if p then q' with the 24 students of class 2 in grade 3 as the universal set. The data will be revealed step by step.
z-m-35-02.thinking.0: Revising your judgment and degree of confidence with new information
z-m-35-02.thinking.1: Telling apart the truth of a proposition when the universal set changes
z-m-35-02.thinking.2: Explaining with the idea of a counterexample
z-m-35-02.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty label for the production batch, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes the learner has already studied the 'sets and propositions' unit of high school Common Mathematics once (operations on sets, the proposition 'if p then q', and counterexamples).
z-m-35-02.prereq.1: That the proposition 'if p then q' is false if there is an element (a counterexample) for which p is true and q is false
z-m-35-02.s.s1.prompt: The data will be revealed one at a time. At each step, choose the most suitable judgment. You do not have to change your judgment from the earlier step.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first count whether there are 'students who satisfy p'.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write down what kind of student there would have to be for it to be 'false', and look for such a student in the current data.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.info: You measured the heights of all 24 students of class 2 in grade 3 and they were from 168 cm to 187 cm. There is not a single student who is 190 cm or taller. There are no records of reading room B use yet.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: With these 24 students as the universal set, how would you judge the proposition 'if a student is 190 cm or taller, they use reading room B'?
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.after: 'If p then q' is false if there is even one element (a counterexample) for which p is true and q is false, and true if there is none. In this class no student satisfies p, so there can be no counterexample, so in mathematics it is regarded as true (b). The feeling in c that 'it never gets to apply' is natural in everyday speech, but remember too that the truth of a proposition is decided this way.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: There is no student 190 cm or taller, so the rule can't be said to hold, so it is false
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: For it to be 'false', there must be a student (a counterexample) for whom p is true and q is false. First check whether such a student can exist in this class.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: There can be no student who goes against it, so it can't be called false, so it is true
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You based it on the fact that if no student satisfies p, a counterexample can't arise.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: There are no students it applies to, so it is hard to say from this class's data whether it is followed
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a common way of speaking in everyday life. But since the truth of a proposition is decided by whether there is a counterexample, go on to think about how to treat the fact that 'there is no counterexample'.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We don't know the records of reading room B use, so we can't make any judgment
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even if you don't know q, if no student satisfies p, no counterexample arises whatever q is. First look at whether there is a student for whom p is true.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Next week a transfer student who is 192 cm tall will join this class. We still don't know whether this student will use reading room B.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: After the transfer student comes, with 25 students as the universal set, what happens if you judge the same proposition now?
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.after: The transfer student satisfies p. If that student does not use reading room B, p is true and q is false, making a counterexample, so the proposition for the 25 students is false, and if the student does use it, there is no counterexample, so it is true. We don't know yet whether the student uses it, so the proposition for the 25 students can't be judged yet, and since one student is enough, there is no need to wait any longer either.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: One transfer student is not enough, so postpone judging until more students 190 cm or taller come
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: One student is enough for a counterexample. Think about why you think a certain number of students must gather before you can judge.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It has already been settled as true in this class, so it won't change even when the transfer student comes
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The truth of a proposition can change with the universal set. Look at what effect it has that the new student satisfies p.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Tall students are expected to use reading room B, so settle it as true now
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Whether a student uses it is a fact confirmed by records, not a guess. Distinguish confirmed information from expectation.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It depends on whether the student uses it. If not, it is false, and if so, it is true
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You pointed out that since there is a student who satisfies p for the first time, whether that student's q is true or false will decide the truth of the proposition.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.info: The transfer student has come, and on checking, they say the student does not use reading room B. The information about the original 24 students has not changed.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would you sum up the proposition for the 25 students and the judgment made for the original 24 students?
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.after: For the 25 students, the transfer student, who is 192 cm and does not use reading room B, is a counterexample, so the proposition is false. The judgment for the original 24 students (true) is still right for that universal set. The judgment was not wrong; the thing it was about changed, and once a counterexample appears, it is false regardless of the other students' records.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is false for the 25 students, and the 'true' for the 24 students is still right for that set
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You distinguished the universal set changing from the first judgment being wrong.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The first judgment was wrong, so the one for the 24 students must be corrected to false too
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Among the 24 there was no student 190 cm or taller, so there was no counterexample. What changed is the universal set.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: There is only one transfer student, so it is mostly followed, so I still regard it as true
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: 'If p then q' is true not when it holds mostly but when there is not a single counterexample. 'It mostly holds' is a different claim.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Postpone judging until the use records of all the other students are confirmed
z-m-35-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The other 24 do not satisfy p. Think about whether their records could change whether there is a counterexample.
z-m-35-02.s.s1.reflect: Over the three steps, what changed and what stayed the same in my judgment? If you distinguish 'there is no case to check' from 'there is no case that goes against it', how does the judgment in the first step change?
z-m-35-02.s.s2.prompt: Using the word 'counterexample', explain to a friend why 'if p then q' is treated as true when no element at all satisfies p. Also add one other example of the same form (a condition on numbers).
z-m-35-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write in one sentence what kind of element there would have to be for 'if p then q' to be false.
z-m-35-02.s.s2.hint.1: Make one condition (about numbers) that no element satisfies p, and test whether the sentence saying that element must exist holds.
z-m-35-02.s.s2.placeholder: Example: For it to be false there would have to be ..., but ...
z-m-35-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did I first say 'what one thing must exist for it to be false'?
z-m-35-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I connect why that thing can't exist with the fact that no element satisfies p?
z-m-35-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is the example I added really a condition that no number satisfies p?
z-m-35-02.s.s2.model.0: Whether it is true or false is decided by whether there is a counterexample. If there is not a single student 190 cm or taller, there can be no such student who does not use reading room B, that is, no counterexample, so it can't be called false, so I regard it as true. As an example of the same form, 'if x is real and x²<0, then x>5' also has no real number with x²<0, so there is no counterexample, so it is true.
z-m-35-02.s.s2.model.1: For "if p then q" to be false, there must be at least one case where p is true and q is wrong. But if there is no case satisfying p at all, such a counterexample cannot exist, so it is true. For example, "if x² < 0 for a real number x, then x > 5" is also true because there is no real x with x² < 0. In terms of sets, it is the same story as the empty set being a subset of any set.
z-m-35-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: Explained by connecting it to sets.

z-m-35-03.title: How many students joined both clubs? What else do we need to know?
z-m-35-03.topic: The number of elements of a union, and the information needed
z-m-35-03.goal: Find the range determined by the relationship between numbers of elements alone, tell apart the information needed to fix the value to one from the information that is not, and build possible situations yourself.
z-m-35-03.material: Of the 40 students in the whole school, 30 are members of club A and 25 are members of club B. There can be students who joined both clubs and students who joined neither club. Let x be the number of students who joined both clubs, and z the number of students who joined neither club. Below, we examine what can be known about x.
z-m-35-03.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-35-03.thinking.1: Checking information that looks useless with an equation
z-m-35-03.thinking.2: Building several possible situations within the constraints
z-m-35-03.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty label for the production batch, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes the learner has already studied the 'sets and propositions' unit of high school Common Mathematics once (operations on sets, the proposition 'if p then q', and counterexamples).
z-m-35-03.prereq.1: The formula for the number of elements of the union of two sets
z-m-35-03.prereq.2: That within the universal set there can be elements that belong to neither set
z-m-35-03.s.s1.prompt: From the information given now (40, 30, 25) alone, what can you say for certain about x?
z-m-35-03.s.s1.hint.0: Assume x is 0 and calculate how many different students joined the two clubs in all.
z-m-35-03.s.s1.hint.1: Change x one value at a time and check whether the 'number of different students who joined' exceeds 40 and whether x exceeds 25.
z-m-35-03.s.s1.r.a: 15 is the value when every student joined at least one club. Check whether that fact was given in the problem.
z-m-35-03.s.s1.o.b: x is not fixed and can be any value from 0 to 25
z-m-35-03.s.s1.r.b: If x is 0, find how many students the total of members comes to and compare it with 40.
z-m-35-03.s.s1.r.c: This judgment uses together the condition that the union cannot exceed the number of students in the whole school and the condition that x cannot exceed the number of members of one club.
z-m-35-03.s.s1.o.d: The information is not enough, so nothing can be said about x
z-m-35-03.s.s1.r.d: Not being fixed to one value does not mean you can't know the range. Test a few possible values yourself.
z-m-35-03.s.s1.explain: The number of elements of A∪B is 30+25−x=55−x, and it cannot exceed the 40 students of the whole school, so 55−x≤40, that is, x≥15. Also x cannot exceed the 25 members of B, so x≤25. Both 15 and 25 are really possible (15 is the case where everyone joined, and 25 is the case where all members of B also joined A), so you can say x is from 15 to 25.
z-m-35-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information below for which knowing just that one more fact fixes x to a single value. (Think of adding each piece of information separately, one at a time.)
z-m-35-03.s.s2.hint.0: Turn each piece of information into an equation or inequality in x.
z-m-35-03.s.s2.hint.1: Sort the result into whether it gives one value of x, gives only a range, or just repeats a fact you already knew.
z-m-35-03.s.s2.o.a: There are 6 students who joined neither club
z-m-35-03.s.s2.r.a: With this information, the number of different students who joined is fixed. Calculate whether you can find x from that number.
z-m-35-03.s.s2.o.b: There are 5 more students who joined only A than students who joined only B
z-m-35-03.s.s2.r.b: Write the two values in terms of x, calculate the difference, and check whether x remains or disappears.
z-m-35-03.s.s2.o.c: Students who joined A or B are at least 80% of the whole school
z-m-35-03.s.s2.r.c: A condition with 'at least' leaves a range, not a single value. Write down a few x that are possible under this condition.
z-m-35-03.s.s2.o.d: There are 10 students who joined only B
z-m-35-03.s.s2.r.d: See whether it can be used right away to find the students among the 25 members of B who also joined A.
z-m-35-03.s.s2.o.e: Of the 40 students in the whole school, 22 are boys
z-m-35-03.s.s2.r.e: Work out whether the information about gender connects to the joining relationship, and if it does, in what way.
z-m-35-03.s.s2.explain: For a, the number of different students who joined is 40−6=34, so 55−x=34 and x=21. For d, the number who joined only B is 25−x=10, so x=15. For b, (30−x)−(25−x)=5 always holds regardless of x, so it is not new information. For c, 55−x≥32, that is, x≤23, so only the range from 15 to 23 remains. e does not connect to the joining relationship.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different situations that satisfy all the conditions. x is the number of students who joined both clubs, and z is the number of students who joined neither club. (A 30 students, B 25 students, whole school 40)
z-m-35-03.s.s3.hint.0: First fix one x, then calculate the number of different students who joined (30+25−x).
z-m-35-03.s.s3.hint.1: Comparing that number with 40 tells you what z must be. Repeat this while changing x.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.var.x: Number of students who joined both clubs
z-m-35-03.s.s3.var.z: Number of students who joined neither club
z-m-35-03.s.s3.ok.c1: Both numbers are integers 0 or greater.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.fail.c1: A number of students must be an integer 0 or greater.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.ok.c2: It does not exceed the number of members of B.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.fail.c2: x cannot be greater than the 25 members of B.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.ok.c3: The number of different students who joined plus the number of students who did not join is 40.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.fail.c3: (30+25−x)+z does not match the 40 students of the whole school.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.explain: z=x−15, so if x is an integer from 15 to 25, z=0 to 10 are paired with it. Examples: (15,0), (18,3), (21,6), (25,10).
z-m-35-03.s.s3.because.prompt: In the three situations you made, how does z change as x gets larger? Explain why, connecting it to the 40 students of the whole school.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.because.hint.0: Change x to 15, 18, 25 and make a table of how z changes.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.because.hint.1: Compare with 40 the fact that 55−x is the number of different students who really joined.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: When x gets larger, z ... because ...
z-m-35-03.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did I say clearly in which direction z goes when x gets larger?
z-m-35-03.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did I use in my reason the fact that the number 55 is a value counted with duplicates?
z-m-35-03.s.s3.because.model.0: When x gets larger, z gets larger too. The more students who joined both clubs, the smaller the number of different students who joined (55−x), so the number of students out of 40 who joined neither club grows.
z-m-35-03.s.s3.because.model.1: z = x − 15, so when x goes up by 1, z goes up by 1 as well. 55 is a value that counts the overlapping students twice, and the students who really joined are 55−x, so the difference from 40 is z.

z-m-35-04.title: When a single value belongs to neither set
z-m-35-04.topic: The truth set of a condition and the boundary value (whether there is an equal sign)
z-m-35-04.goal: Check where the boundary value belongs in the truth set of an inequality condition to judge whether 'or' is always true, and build several cases yourself that satisfy the given constraints in a condition where the position of the equal sign has changed.
z-m-35-04.material: For a real number x, set conditions and their truth sets as follows. [가] p: x<a, q: x>b. [나] p: x<a, q: x≥b. Here a and b are constants, and P and Q are the truth sets of p and q respectively. Minjae solved the case a=b=3 in [가] like this. (How to read: ≥ means 'greater than or equal to', and x<a means 'x is less than a'.)
z-m-35-04.thinking.0: Finding the case missed in the solution
z-m-35-04.thinking.2: Building several solutions within the constraints
z-m-35-04.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty label for the production batch, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes the learner has already studied the 'sets and propositions' unit of high school Common Mathematics once (operations on sets, the proposition 'if p then q', and counterexamples).
z-m-35-04.prereq.1: Showing the truth sets of the inequalities x<a and x≥b on a number line
z-m-35-04.prereq.2: That the truth set of the condition 'p or q' is P∪Q
z-m-35-04.s.s1.line.0: Let a=b=3. Then p is x<3 and q is x>3.
z-m-35-04.s.s1.line.1: If x is less than 3, p is true, and if x is greater than 3, q is true.
z-m-35-04.s.s1.line.2: The case x=3 is neither less than nor greater than 3, so it belongs to neither side and we do not need to consider it separately.
z-m-35-04.s.s1.line.3: Therefore, for all real numbers x, 'p or q' is true.
z-m-35-04.s.s1.explain: The problem is that in line 3 it states itself that x=3 belongs to neither condition and then says 'we do not need to consider it separately'. 'For all real numbers x' includes x=3 as well, and if both p and q are false at x=3, then 'p or q' is false, so in [가] you can't say that if a=b it is true for all real numbers. The conclusion in line 4 is wrong because of line 3.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.prompt: Now, in [나] (p: x<a, q: x≥b), make 3 different pairs (a, b) that satisfy all of the following. (i) 'p or q' is true for all real numbers x. (ii) There are exactly 2 integers x that satisfy both p and q at the same time. a and b may be decimals.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.hint.0: Draw P and Q on a number line and decide where b and a must be for them to connect without a gap.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.hint.1: List the integers in the interval from b up to but not including a, and adjust a and b so that there are exactly 2.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.ok.c1: No real number is left out (condition (i)).
z-m-35-04.s.s2.fail.c1: If b is greater than a, numbers from a up to but not including b satisfy neither p nor q.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.ok.c2: There are exactly 2 integers from b up to but not including a (condition (ii)).
z-m-35-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of integers from b up to but not including a is not 2.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.explain: In [나], P is below a and Q is b or above. For the union to be all real numbers, b≤a is needed, and the numbers satisfying both at once are those from b up to but not including a. It is enough that there are exactly 2 integers in there, so for example (3,1) contains 1, 2, (2.5,0.5) contains 1, 2, and (4.2,2.3) contains 3, 4. If b=a, there are no overlapping numbers at all, so (ii) is not satisfied.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain how P and Q are related in [나] when b=a, and how that is different from why the same a=b was a problem in [가].
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Set a=b=3 and put x=3 into p and q of [나], and write whether each is true or false.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare it with putting the same x=3 into p and q of [가].
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: In [나], x=a goes into ... so ...
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did I say which set x=a belongs to, separately for [나] and [가]?
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I point out that P and Q are complements of each other or that there is no overlapping number?
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.model.0: In [나], if a=b, P is below a and Q is a or above, so x=a goes into Q. So the union is all the real numbers, and no x overlaps, so they are complements of each other. In [가], q has no equal sign, so x=a goes into neither P nor Q.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.model.1: What differs is who gets the boundary value x=a. In [나], q is 'greater than or equal to', so it includes a and there is no gap, but [가] is 'greater than', so a is left out. So in [가], even if a=b, it is not always true.
z-m-35-04.s.s1.prompt: Where is the first line in Minjae's solution where the logic goes wrong? Count line numbers from 1.
z-m-35-04.s.s1.hint.0: Using the p and q set in line 1, classify each real number as belonging to p or q.
z-m-35-04.s.s1.hint.1: Think about which x are included in "for every real number x," and check line by line whether each line dealt with all those x.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.model.2: In [나], when b=a, P is x<a and Q is x≥a, so they split all the real numbers with no overlap, but in [가], x=3 belongs to neither P nor Q, so the union is not all the real numbers.
z-m-35-04.s.s2.because.modelNote.2: An answer written with the specific value x=3

z-m-35-05.title: Two sentences with the same words in a different order: do they mean the same?
z-m-35-05.topic: The order in propositions that have both 'every' and 'some'
z-m-35-05.goal: Use a table to check that two sentences differing in the order of 'for every ... there is' and 'some ... every' do not imply each other, and find the wrong connection and explain it with a counterexample.
z-m-35-05.material: Four students 가, 나, 다, 라 sent each other cheer notes. No one sent one to themselves. Each line of the table is 'sender → recipients'. [Table 1] 가→나, 다, 라 / 나→다 / 다→나 / 라→다. [Table 2] 가→나 / 나→다 / 다→라 / 라→가. Statement ㄱ: For every student, there is a student who sent a note to that student. Statement ㄴ: Some student sent a note to every other student.
z-m-35-05.thinking.0: Reading evidence from a table to judge
z-m-35-05.thinking.2: Explaining a logical relationship with counterexamples
z-m-35-05.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty label for the production batch, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes the learner has already studied the 'sets and propositions' unit of high school Common Mathematics once (operations on sets, the proposition 'if p then q', and counterexamples).
z-m-35-05.prereq.1: The meaning of 'for every x' and 'there exists an x such that'
z-m-35-05.s.s1.hint.0: Read the table by sender line for ㄴ, and one recipient at a time for ㄱ.
z-m-35-05.s.s1.hint.1: To check ㄱ, write one at a time whether there is a student who sent to each of 가, 나, 다, 라.
z-m-35-05.s.s1.r.a: For ㄱ you have to examine the 'receiving side' for each student. Read the table vertically and check whether there is a student who received from no one.
z-m-35-05.s.s1.o.b: Both ㄱ and ㄴ are true
z-m-35-05.s.s1.r.b: Check whether the two statements read the table in the same direction. ㄱ looks at the receiving side, and ㄴ looks at the sending side.
z-m-35-05.s.s1.o.c: Both ㄱ and ㄴ are false
z-m-35-05.s.s1.r.c: When checking ㄴ, look line by line at whether one line includes all of the other three students.
z-m-35-05.s.s1.r.d: This is the result of checking, on the sender's line, whether one student sent to all the others, and checking separately, on the receiving side, whether every student received one.
z-m-35-05.s.s1.explain: In [Table 1], 가 sent to all of 나, 다, 라, so ㄴ is true. But no one sent a note to 가, so ㄱ is false.
z-m-35-05.s.s2.prompt: Harin claimed that ㄴ is also true in [Table 2] and explained as below. Which line is the first where the logic goes wrong? Line numbers are counted from 1.
z-m-35-05.s.s2.hint.0: In [Table 2], check line by line whether 가's line includes all of the other three students.
z-m-35-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare with the sentence of ㄴ the point that in ㄱ, the 'sender' for each student may be the same student or a different one.
z-m-35-05.s.s2.line.0: In [Table 2], 가 sent to 나, 나 sent to 다, 다 sent to 라, and 라 sent to 가.
z-m-35-05.s.s2.line.1: Looking at the receiving side, each of 가, 나, 다, 라 received a note once, so ㄱ is true.
z-m-35-05.s.s2.line.2: Each student having received a note means there is a sender for each student, so it follows that some one student sent to all the other students.
z-m-35-05.s.s2.line.3: Therefore ㄴ is also true in [Table 2].
z-m-35-05.s.s2.explain: Up to line 2 it is right (ㄱ is true in [Table 2]). Line 3 goes wrong in saying that from 'for every student there is a sender' (the sender may differ for each recipient), 'one student sent to everyone' (the same sender for everyone) follows. In [Table 2], every student sent to exactly one person, so ㄴ is false. The conclusion in line 4 is wrong because of line 3.
z-m-35-05.s.s3.prompt: Based on the two tables, judge whether 'if ㄴ is true then ㄱ is necessarily true' and 'if ㄱ is true then ㄴ is necessarily true' each always hold, and write which table is the evidence for each judgment.
z-m-35-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write whether ㄱ and ㄴ are true or false in [Table 1], and do the same for [Table 2].
z-m-35-05.s.s3.hint.1: Use the fact that if there is a table where one is true and the other is false, the 'necessarily' in that direction is broken.
z-m-35-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Even if ㄴ is true, ㄱ ... in Table 1 ...
z-m-35-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I judge each of the two directions (ㄴ→ㄱ, ㄱ→ㄴ) separately?
z-m-35-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In the tables I gave, did I point out concretely that one statement is true and the other is false?
z-m-35-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I say in my own words that the meaning changes if the order of 'every' and 'some' is different?
z-m-35-05.s.s3.model.0: Neither always holds. In Table 1, ㄴ is true but ㄱ is false because no one sent to 가. In Table 2, ㄱ is true but ㄴ is false (every sender sent to only one person). So there is one counterexample for each.
z-m-35-05.s.s3.model.1: Even if ㄴ is true, there is no guarantee that ㄱ is true (Table 1 is a counterexample), and even if ㄱ is true, there is no guarantee that ㄴ is true (Table 2 is a counterexample). That each student has a sender and that one student sent to everyone mean different things because the order of 'every' and 'some' is different.
z-m-35-05.s.s3.model.2: In table 1, ㄴ is true and ㄱ is false, and in table 2, ㄱ is true and ㄴ is false, so neither is guaranteed.

z-m-35-06.title: Building two conditions yourself with a fixed number of counterexamples
z-m-35-06.topic: Counting counterexamples of the proposition 'if p then q' and of its converse (inclusion of truth sets)
z-m-35-06.goal: Use the fact that the difference of the truth sets is the set of counterexamples to design yourself two conditions that satisfy constraints on the number of counterexamples, and compare the several solutions.
z-m-35-06.material: With the universal set U={1, 2, 3, …, 12}, consider two conditions p: x≥a, q: x≤b. a and b are integers from 1 to 12, and P and Q are the truth sets of p and q respectively. A counterexample to the proposition 'if p then q' is an element of U for which p is true and q is false, and a counterexample to its converse 'if q then p' is an element for which q is true and p is false. (How to read: x≥a is 'x is at least a', and x≤b is 'x is at most b'.)
z-m-35-06.thinking.1: Designing conditions that satisfy the constraints
z-m-35-06.thinking.2: Comparing the structure of different solutions
z-m-35-06.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty label for the production batch, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes the learner has already studied the 'sets and propositions' unit of high school Common Mathematics once (operations on sets, the proposition 'if p then q', and counterexamples).
z-m-35-06.prereq.1: Truth sets and the subset relation
z-m-35-06.prereq.2: The converse of a proposition, 'if q then p'
z-m-35-06.s.s1.prompt: Which one best expresses the counterexamples of the proposition 'if p then q' using the truth sets P and Q?
z-m-35-06.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one or two elements of U yourself that fit the meaning of a counterexample ('the condition p is true but the conclusion q is false').
z-m-35-06.s.s1.hint.1: Write down which of P and Q that element belongs to and which it does not belong to.
z-m-35-06.s.s1.o.a: An element that belongs to P and does not belong to Q (P−Q)
z-m-35-06.s.s1.r.a: You translated the meaning of a counterexample, 'p is true but q is false', into the language of sets.
z-m-35-06.s.s1.o.b: An element that belongs to Q and does not belong to P (Q−P)
z-m-35-06.s.s1.r.b: These elements are the ones that break 'if q then p'. Look again at the fact that a counterexample is an element where 'the condition side is true and the conclusion side is false'.
z-m-35-06.s.s1.o.c: An element that belongs to both P and Q (P∩Q)
z-m-35-06.s.s1.r.c: An element for which both p and q are true does not break 'if p then q' and actually supports it. Compare with the meaning of a counterexample.
z-m-35-06.s.s1.o.d: An element that belongs to neither P nor Q
z-m-35-06.s.s1.r.d: Compare with the meaning of a counterexample what role an element for which both p and q are false plays in 'if p then q'.
z-m-35-06.s.s1.explain: A counterexample to 'if p then q' is an element for which p is true and q is false, that is, an element that belongs to P and does not belong to Q, so it is P−Q (=P∩Qᶜ). A counterexample to the converse 'if q then p' is Q−P.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different (a, b) that satisfy all the following conditions. (i) There are exactly 3 counterexamples to 'if p then q' in U. (ii) The converse 'if q then p' has at least 1 counterexample and fewer than 3.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.hint.0: Fix one a and b, write P and Q out with numbers from 1 to 12, and count the numbers that belong only to P.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.hint.1: For there to be 3 numbers that belong only to P, decide where P must start and where Q must end, and then check how many numbers belong only to Q.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.ok.c0: a and b are integers from 1 to 12.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.fail.c0: a and b must be integers from 1 to 12.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.ok.c1: There are exactly 3 counterexamples to 'if p then q'.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of counterexamples to 'if p then q' is not 3.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The converse has at least 1 counterexample.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The converse has fewer than 3 counterexamples.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The converse has 3 or more counterexamples.
z-m-35-06.s.s2.explain: P={a, …, 12}, Q={1, …, b}. P−Q is the numbers from max(a, b+1) to 12, so for the count to be 3, max(a, b+1)=10. Also Q−P is the numbers from 1 to min(b, a−1), so the number of counterexamples to the converse is min(b, a−1), and it must be 1 or 2. The possible pairs are only the four (2,9), (3,9), (10,1), (10,2).
z-m-35-06.s.s3.prompt: Choose two of the pairs (a, b) you found that have different shapes, compare how P and Q lie in the list of numbers (whether they overlap or are separate), and write why the two pairs satisfy the conditions.
z-m-35-06.s.s3.hint.0: For each pair you found, write P and Q using the numbers 1 to 12 and check whether any number is in both sets.
z-m-35-06.s.s3.hint.1: If they have different shapes, compare which set sits at one end.
z-m-35-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: For (2, 9), P is ..., and for (10, 1), ...
z-m-35-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: For the two pairs, did I write concretely the numbers that belong only to P and only to Q?
z-m-35-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I say clearly how the shapes of the two pairs differ (whether they overlap)?
z-m-35-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I check whether there are other pairs I missed?
z-m-35-06.s.s3.model.0: If (a, b)=(2, 9), P is 2 to 12 and Q is 1 to 9, so they overlap. The 10, 11, 12 that are only in P are the 3 counterexamples, and the 1 that is only in Q is 1 counterexample to the converse. If (10, 1), P is 10 to 12 and Q is just 1, so they are separate, the 10, 11, 12 only in P are the 3 counterexamples, and the 1 only in Q is 1 counterexample to the converse.
z-m-35-06.s.s3.model.1: If a=3, b=9, P is 3 or more and Q is 9 or less, so the overlapping part is 3 to 9, the part only in P is 10, 11, 12 (3 numbers), and the part only in Q is 1, 2 (2 numbers). The 2 counterexamples to the converse are fewer than 3. If a=10, b=2, then P (10 to 12) and Q (1 to 2) do not overlap, with 3 numbers only in P and 2 numbers only in Q.
